data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The surviving view is that the preference is defensible as a non-inductive 'verisimilitude' heuristic, but accepting it costs the certainty that science converges on truth, leaving us with only 'boldness' as a guide.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If verisimilitude cannot be formally defined or measured without invoking probability, the defense collapses.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'cost' includes the inability to justify why we should trust technology built on these theories, the position becomes pragmatically untenable.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the evolutionary analogy requires an inductive assumption that the 'fitness landscape' of truth is stable, the smuggling charge stands.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Popper later introduced 'verisimilitude' (truth-likeness) to explain why we prefer corroborated theories: they seem closer to the truth. The mechanism is evolutionary: we select theories that have survived severe filters. This is defensible without induction if viewed as a search strategy in a landscape of errors. However, the cost is high: we can never know if we are actually getting closer to the truth or just finding theories that fit current local conditions. We lose the guarantee of progress, retaining only the hope that eliminating error leaves something better behind.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
